short: An underground stem that grows horizontally; the part of ginger that is harvested.
A plant known only in cultivation, with no wild population.
One of the two sets of chromosomes an organism inherits; a haplotype-resolved genome separates them.
The main pungent compounds of fresh ginger; 6-gingerol is the most abundant.
Pungent compounds formed from gingerols when ginger is dried or heated.
A protein-digesting enzyme in ginger rhizome that tenderises meat.
A receptor on sensory nerves that responds to heat and to pungent compounds such as capsaicin and gingerols.
A serotonin receptor in the gut and brain that standard anti-nausea drugs block.
A compound to which the body has attached a sugar acid, usually making it easier to excrete.
Breakdown of a swallowed compound in the gut wall and liver before it reaches the general circulation.
A statistical pooling of the results of several studies of the same question.
A review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
A system for rating how certain a body of evidence is, from very low to high.
The extent to which pooled studies disagree with one another, often reported as I².
The range of values compatible with a study's data; a wide interval means an imprecise estimate.
The pre-modern medical doctrine that health is a balance of four humours with qualities of hot, cold, wet and dry.
The exact preparation a study gave its participants.
The mix of compounds a plant releases from its roots into the surrounding soil.
"The three pungents": long pepper, black pepper and ginger used together in Ayurvedic medicine.
A medieval spiced wine, sweetened and flavoured with a powder of cinnamon, ginger and other spices.
The gelatinous starter used to brew home ginger beer; a partnership of a yeast and a bacterium.
An enzyme that builds a carbon chain by joining small units; in ginger, the type III enzyme ZoPKS2 makes the gingerol skeleton.
The plant pathway that turns the amino acid phenylalanine into ferulic acid and related compounds, the start of gingerol biosynthesis.
The product of the condensation step in gingerol biosynthesis; two reductions are thought to turn it into 6-gingerol.
A milder-smelling compound formed from gingerol by heat or alkali, not a natural constituent of fresh ginger.
A protein that switches genes on or off by binding near them; in ginger, some control genes of the gingerol pathway.
The set of genes being expressed in a tissue at a given time, measured by sequencing its RNA.
Having four sets of chromosomes instead of the usual two (diploid); some ginger lines have been doubled this way.
Raising plants from small pieces of tissue in sterile culture, a way to start ginger free of soil-borne disease.
Supplying fertiliser dissolved in irrigation water, often to plants grown in soilless substrates.
A rot of ginger rhizomes caused mainly by Pythium species, one of the most damaging diseases of the crop.
A wilting disease of ginger caused by Ralstonia bacteria, which block the plant's water-conducting tissue.
A microbe that lives inside a plant's tissues without harming it, and may help it grow.
The volatile, aromatic fraction of a plant, distilled or extracted; in ginger it carries the citrus and woody aroma, not the heat.
An enzyme that makes the terpenes of a plant's essential oil.
The lemon-scented aroma compound of fresh ginger, a mixture of geranial and neral.
Severe, persistent vomiting in pregnancy, beyond ordinary morning sickness, often needing hospital care.
A trial in which each participant receives both treatments in turn, so that each acts as their own comparison.
An inactive dummy given to the comparison group in a trial so that participants cannot tell which treatment they have.
A ginger preparation made to contain a set amount of named compounds, unlike plain powdered rhizome.
How a substance is absorbed, changed, distributed and removed by the body over time.
In EU herbal law, a use accepted on published clinical evidence, as against traditional use, accepted on long-standing use.
A reference work listing medicinal substances and their uses; also the body of knowledge such books record.
A compound released by platelets that makes them clump; lower levels suggest reduced platelet activity.
The enzyme that starts the making of leukotrienes, inflammatory signals; ginger compounds inhibit it in the laboratory.
The rate at which the stomach passes its contents on to the intestine, usually given as a half-emptying time.
Pyridoxine, a vitamin used as a first treatment for pregnancy sickness and as the comparison in several ginger trials.
A standard anti-sickness drug used as the comparison in early ginger trials.
An anticoagulant whose effect is easily changed by other substances, so it is used to test for interactions.
Glycated haemoglobin, a blood test reflecting average blood sugar over the previous two to three months.
